cards.title: Question Tags
rule: Definition: Question Tags & Short Additions (ሕቶኣዊ ጭራታትን ሓጸርቲ መወሰኽታታትን) are syntactic structures used to seek confirmation at the end of a statement (question tags) or to express agreement or disagreement with a previous statement (short additions) using auxiliary matching and subject-verb inversion.

Question tags (ሕቶኣዊ ጭራታት) are short clauses appended to declarative or imperative sentences to transform them into questions. The foundational rule of tag formation is polarity opposition: a positive statement requires a negative tag ($$\text{Positive Statement} \rightarrow \text{Negative Tag}$$), and a negative statement requires a positive tag ($$\text{Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag}$$). Tigrinya possesses no direct equivalent to this matching system; instead, it utilizes invariant terminal expressions such as "ኣይኮነን?" (isn't it?) or the question particle "-ዶ" regardless of the subject, verb, or polarity of the preceding clause (e.g., "ንሱ መምህር እዩ፡ ኣይኮነን?" and "ንሳቶም ከይዶም እዮም፡ ኣይኮነን?"). This lack of structural variation in L1 causes Tigrinya-speaking students to overgeneralize and write "isn't it?" or "no?" at the end of all English statements, making tag formation a heavily tested diagnostic area on national exams.

To construct a grammatically correct question tag, the auxiliary verb of the tag must match the auxiliary verb of the main clause in tense, aspect, and number. If the main clause does not contain an auxiliary verb (as in active simple present or simple past clauses), the tag must introduce dummy do-support ($$\text{Simple Present} \rightarrow \text{don't/doesn't}$$ and $$\text{Simple Past} \rightarrow \text{didn't}$$ — e.g. "She works here, *doesn't she*?", "They left early, *didn't they*?").

cards.title: Notes
body: Definition: Question Tags & Short Additions (ሕቶኣዊ ጭራታትን ሓጸርቲ መወሰኽታታትን) are syntactic structures used to seek confirmation at the end of a statement (question tags) or to express agreement or disagreement with a previous statement (short additions) using auxiliary matching and subject-verb inversion.

Question tags (ሕቶኣዊ ጭራታት) are short clauses appended to declarative or imperative sentences to transform them into questions. The foundational rule of tag formation is polarity opposition: a positive statement requires a negative tag ($$\text{Positive Statement} \rightarrow \text{Negative Tag}$$), and a negative statement requires a positive tag ($$\text{Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag}$$). Tigrinya possesses no direct equivalent to this matching system; instead, it utilizes invariant terminal expressions such as "ኣይኮነን?" (isn't it?) or the question particle "-ዶ" regardless of the subject, verb, or polarity of the preceding clause (e.g., "ንሱ መምህር እዩ፡ ኣይኮነን?" and "ንሳቶም ከይዶም እዮም፡ ኣይኮነን?"). This lack of structural variation in L1 causes Tigrinya-speaking students to overgeneralize and write "isn't it?" or "no?" at the end of all English statements, making tag formation a heavily tested diagnostic area on national exams.

To construct a grammatically correct question tag, the auxiliary verb of the tag must match the auxiliary verb of the main clause in tense, aspect, and number. If the main clause does not contain an auxiliary verb (as in active simple present or simple past clauses), the tag must introduce dummy do-support ($$\text{Simple Present} \rightarrow \text{don't/doesn't}$$ and $$\text{Simple Past} \rightarrow \text{didn't}$$ — e.g. "She works here, *doesn't she*?", "They left early, *didn't they*?").

Several irregular patterns and syntactic exceptions are common filters on the matriculation exam. The first-person singular copula "I am" requires the irregular negative tag aren't I? (e.g., "I am late, *aren't I*?"). However, the negative statement "I am not" follows the regular pattern, taking "am I?" (e.g., "I am not late, *am I*?"). Suggestions starting with "Let's" require the tag shall we? (e.g., "Let's take a break, *shall we*?"). Imperatives usually take *will you?* or *won't you?* (e.g., "Close the door, *will you*?"), and statements with negative words such as *never, hardly, nobody* take a positive tag (e.g., "He never comes late, *does he*?").

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I am late for the registration of the national matriculation examination, ________?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The main clause starts with the positive first-person singular copula 'I am'. This requires an irregular negative question tag in standard English: $$\text{I am} \rightarrow \text{aren't I?}$$.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'am not I' (Option A) because they try to follow regular polarity rules, or 'isn't it' (Option D) due to L1 transfer. Option B 'aren't I' is the correct irregular grammatical exception.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ወግዓዊ ሰዋስው፡ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ብ 'I am' (ኣነ...) ምስ ዝጅምር፡ እቲ ናቱ ፍሉይ ሕቶኣዊ ጭራ (question tag) ወትሩ 'aren't I?' (Option B - ኣይኮንኩን?) እዩ ዝኸውን። 'am not I' ምጥቃም ዓቢ ጌጋ እዩ ምኽንያቱ ከምዚ ዝበለ መዋቕር ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ሰዋስው ስለ ዘየለ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She rarely visits her relatives in Gondar during the long academic vacations, ________?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The adverb 'rarely' is semi-negative, which makes the main statement grammatically negative. This requires a positive question tag with present simple dummy do-support ($$\text{Semi-Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often see the positive verb spelling 'visits' and automatically select a negative tag like 'doesn't she' (Option A). However, because 'rarely' is negative, the positive tag 'does she' (Option B) is correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Rarely' (ሳሕቲ/ኣዝዩ ውሑድ ግዜ) ዝብል ቃል ኣሉታዊ ቃና (semi-negative) ስለ ዘለዎ፡ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ከም ኣሉታዊ ይውሰድ። ስለዚ እቲ ዝስዕብ ሕቶኣዊ ጭራ ብኣዎንታዊ ሓገዝቲ ግሲ 'does she' (Option B) ክኸውን ኣለዎ። 'doesn't she' ምምራጽ ናይዚ ሕጊ መጻወድያ እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She rarely ever goes to cinema_______?
cards.why: The word 'rarely' is semi-negative, which makes the whole sentence negative. Negative sentences require positive question tags. Since the verb is 'goes' (Present Simple), the tag is 'does she'.

questions.q: I am late for the registration of the national matriculation examination, ________?
questions.label: 1. I am late for the registration of the national matriculation
why: The main clause starts with the positive first-person singular copula 'I am'. This requires an irregular negative question tag in standard English: $$\text{I am} \rightarrow \text{aren't I?}$$.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: She rarely visits her relatives in Gondar during the long academic vacations, ________?
questions.label: 2. She rarely visits her relatives in Gondar during the long ac
why: The adverb 'rarely' is semi-negative, which makes the main statement grammatically negative. This requires a positive question tag with present simple dummy do-support ($$\text{Semi-Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag}$$).
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: Everyone was extremely excited about the university scholarship announcement, ________?
questions.label: 3. Everyone was extremely excited about the university scholars
why: Indefinite pronouns referring to people ('everyone') require the plural pronoun 'they' in the tag. Because the pronoun is plural, the past copula 'was' must shift to plural 'weren't' to maintain agreement.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: Let's take a brief walk in the school garden before the final lecture begins, ________?
questions.label: 4. Let's take a brief walk in the school garden before the fina
why: Suggestions starting with 'Let's' (contraction of 'Let us') require the irregular question tag 'shall we?' in standard English.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.label: 5. She doesn't speak French fluently, ________?
why: The main clause is negative ('doesn't speak'). This requires a positive question tag using the matching auxiliary 'does': $$\text{Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag}$$.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q:
Speaker A: 'I really love studying English literature.' 
Speaker B: '________'
questions.label:
6. Speaker A: 'I really love studying English literature.' 
Spe
why: Speaker A's statement is positive and in the Simple Present tense (no auxiliary present). Speaker B wants to show agreement, requiring the inverted positive agreement structure: $$\text{So} + \text{do/does} + \text{Subject}$$.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q:
Speaker A: 'I don't like drinking hot tea in the afternoon.' 
Speaker B: '________'
questions.label: 7. Speaker A: 'I don't like drinking hot tea in the afternoon.'
why: Speaker A's statement is negative ('don't like'). To show agreement with a negative statement, Speaker B must use the inverted negative agreement structure: $$\text{Neither/Nor} + \text{Auxiliary} + \text{Subject}$$.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: Nothing went wrong during the school laboratory experiment, ________?
questions.label: 8. Nothing went wrong during the school laboratory experiment,
why: The subject 'Nothing' is negative, which makes the main statement grammatically negative. This requires a positive question tag with past simple dummy do-support and the singular pronoun 'it' ($$\text{Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag wi
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: Don't make any noise while the national exam is in progress, ________?
questions.label: 9. Don't make any noise while the national exam is in progress,
why: Negative imperatives (commands starting with 'Don't') strictly require the positive tag 'will you?' in standard English.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: The university dean has already signed the official graduation list, ________?
questions.label: 10. The university dean has already signed the official graduati
why: The main clause contains the positive perfect auxiliary 'has' ('has already signed'). This requires a negative question tag with the matching auxiliary 'hasn't' and pronoun 'he': $$\text{Positive Statement} \rightarrow \text{Negative Tag}$$.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: Punctuation marks are very important in writing, _______?
why:
To form a question tag:
1. Use the auxiliary verb from the statement ('are').
2. If the statement is positive, the tag must be negative ('aren't').
3. Use the pronoun that corresponds to the subject ('Punctuation marks' = 'they').
Result: **'aren't they'**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: None of the students is trying, ___________?
why: The word 'None' makes the sentence negative, so the question tag must be positive. Since 'students' is plural, the pronoun 'they' is used. Therefore, 'Are they' is the correct tag.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Selam: I hope it is going to be a minor surgery, **61**?
why: **Rule:** A question tag uses the auxiliary verb from the main sentence. Since the main sentence is positive ('it **is** going to be'), the tag must be negative: **'isn't it?'**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Only two students understood the instruction, ___?
why: The main sentence is positive and in the Simple Past ('understood'). Therefore, the question tag must be negative and use the auxiliary 'did' ('didn't they').
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Suleman: This coat looks nice for such a chilly weather, __________?
why: **Rule:** For a positive statement in Present Simple ("This coat looks"), the tag must be negative using the auxiliary 'do/does'. Since "coat" is singular, we use "doesn't it".
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

why: For imperative sentences (commands or requests), 'will you' is the most common and standard question tag used to invite cooperation.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Don't open the question paper until you are told to do so, _____________?
why: For negative imperatives (commands starting with 'Don't'), the standard question tag is 'will you'.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: All the teachers are working hard this semester, (38) ______.
why: To add a positive statement that agree with a previous positive statement, we use 'so + auxiliary verb + subject'. Since the first clause uses 'are', the addition is 'so are the students'.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.
